danish.title: Sjette bog (1808–10) — Kapitel 1
paragraphs: Fyrst Andrej havde tilbragt to år uafbrudt på landet.

Alle de planer, Pierre havde forsøgt at gennemføre på sine godser — og som han ustandselig skiftede mellem uden nogensinde at fuldføre — blev gennemført af fyrst Andrej uden ståhej og uden mærkbar anstrengelse.
Han besad i højeste grad den praktiske udholdenhed, som Pierre manglede, og uden hastværk eller pres fra hans side kom tingene i gang.

På et af sine godser blev de tre hundrede livegne frigivet og blev frie landbrugere — et af de første eksempler af sin art i Rusland. På andre godser blev bøndernes tvangsarbejde omregnet til en pengeafgift. En uddannet jordemoder blev ansat på Bogutjarovo for hans regning, og en præst blev betalt for at undervise bøndernes og husfolkenes børn i læsning og skrivning.

Fyrst Andrej tilbragte halvdelen af sin tid på Lysye Gory hos sin far og sin søn, der stadig var i ammernes varetægt. Den anden halvdel tilbragte han i »Bogutjarovo-klosteret«, som hans far kaldte fyrst Andrejs gods. Trods den ligegyldighed over for verdens anliggender, han havde udtrykt over for Pierre, fulgte han flittigt med i alt, hvad der skete, modtog mange bøger og opdagede til sin overraskelse, at når han eller hans far fik besøg fra Sankt Petersborg, selve livets centrum, hang disse folk efter ham — der aldrig forlod landet — i viden om, hvad der foregik inden- og udenrigs.

Foruden at beskæftige sig med sine godser og at læse et stort udvalg af bøger var fyrst Andrej på denne tid optaget af en kritisk gennemgang af vores seneste to uheldige felttog og af at udarbejde et forslag til reform af hærens regler og bestemmelser.
I foråret 1809 tog han til Rjazan-godserne, som hans søn havde arvet, og hvis værge han var.

Varmet af forårssolen sad han i kaleschen og betragtede det nye græs, de første blade på birkene og de første pust af hvide forårssky, der svævede hen over den klare blå himmel. Han tænkte ikke på noget, men så adspredt og muntert til begge sider.

De krydsede færgestedet, hvor han havde talt med Pierre året forinden. De kørte gennem den mudrede landsby, forbi tærskepladser og grønne marker med vintersæd, ned ad bakke, hvor der endnu lå sne nær broen, op ad bakke, hvor regnen havde gjort leret flydende, forbi strimler af stubjord og buske, der hist og her var berørt af grønt, og ind i en birkeskov, der voksede på begge sider af vejen. I skoven var det næsten varmt, ingen vind kunne mærkes. Birkene med deres klæbrige grønne blade stod ubevægelige, og lilla blomster og de første grønne strå skød op og løftede fjorårets blade. De stedsegrønne fyretræers grove farve, spredt hist og her mellem birkene, var en ubehagelig påmindelse om vinteren. Da de kørte ind i skoven, begyndte hestene at snøfte og svedte synligt.
Tjeneren Pjotr sagde noget til kusken; denne nikkede. Men tilsyneladende var kuskens tilslutning ikke nok for Pjotr, og han vendte sig på bukken mod sin herre.
»Hvor dejligt det er, Deres højvelbårenhed!« sagde han med et ærbødigt smil.
»Hvad?«
»Det er dejligt, Deres højvelbårenhed!«

»Hvad taler han om?« tænkte fyrst Andrej. »Åh, foråret, tænker jeg,« sagde han til sig selv, idet han drejede sig om. »Ja, rigtig nok er alting grønt allerede... Hvor tidligt! Birkene og kirsebær og ellene er også ved at springe ud... Men egene viser ingen tegn endnu. Ah, dér er en eg!«

Ved vejkanten stod en eg. Den var nok ti gange ældre end de birke, der udgjorde skoven, ti gange tykkere og dobbelt så høj. Det var et enormt træ, hvis omkreds var dobbelt så stor som en mand kunne omfavne, og det var tydeligt, at nogle af dets grene for længst var knækket af og barken arret. Med sine vældige, uskønne lemmer, der bredte sig usymmetrisk ud, og sine krogede hænder og fingre stod det som et gammelt, strengt og foragteligt uhyre blandt de smilende birketræer. Kun de dødsagtige, stedsegrønne fyrretræer, spredt rundt i skoven, og denne eg nægtede at give efter for forårstrylleri eller lægge mærke til hverken foråret eller solskinnet.

»Forår, kærlighed, lykke!« syntes denne eg at sige. »Er I ikke trætte af den dumme, meningsløse, evigt gentagne svindel? Altid det samme og altid svindel? Der er intet forår, ingen sol, ingen lykke! Se på de sammenpressede, døde fyrretræer, altid de samme, og på mig, der stikker mine knækkede og afbarkede fingre ud, præcis hvor de er vokset, fra min ryg eller mine sider: som de er vokset, sådan står jeg, og jeg tror ikke på jeres håb og jeres løgne.«

Da han kørte gennem skoven, drejede fyrst Andrej sig flere gange for at se på den eg, som om han ventede noget af den. Under egen var der også blomster og græs, men den stod mellem dem, sammenbidt, stiv, misdannet og dyster som altid.
»Ja, egen har ret, tusind gange ret,« tænkte fyrst Andrej. »Lad andre — de unge — give efter for den svindel igen, men vi kender livet, vores liv er forbi!«

En hel række nye tanker, håbløse men vemodigt behagelige, steg op i hans sjæl i forbindelse med det træ. Under denne rejse gennemtænkte han så at sige sit liv på ny og nåede frem til sin gamle slutning, der beroligede ved sin håbløshed: at det ikke var for ham at begynde noget nyt — men at han måtte leve sit liv ud, tilfreds med ikke at gøre skade og uden at forstyrre sig selv eller ønske noget.

english.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 1
paragraphs: Prince Andrew had spent two years continuously in the country.

All the plans Pierre had attempted on his estates — constantly switching from one thing to another without finishing any of them — were carried out by Prince Andrew quietly and without apparent effort.
He possessed to the highest degree a practical tenacity that Pierre lacked, and without fuss or strain this quality set things in motion.

On one of his estates, three hundred serfs were liberated and became free agricultural laborers — one of the first such examples in Russia. On other estates, the serfs' compulsory labor was replaced by a cash payment. A trained midwife was hired for Bogucharovo at his expense, and a priest was paid to teach the peasants' and household serfs' children reading and writing.

Prince Andrew spent half his time at Bald Hills with his father and his son, who was still in the care of nurses. The other half he spent in "Bogucharovo Cloister," as his father called Prince Andrew's estate. Despite the indifference to the world's affairs he had professed to Pierre, he diligently followed everything that was happening. He received many books and was surprised to find that when visitors came from Petersburg — the very center of life — they were actually behind him, despite his never leaving the country, in their knowledge of both domestic and foreign affairs.

Besides managing his estates and reading widely, Prince Andrew was at this time working on a critical analysis of the two most recent, unsuccessful campaigns and drafting a proposal for reforming the army's rules and regulations.
In the spring of 1809 he went to visit the Ryazan estates that his son had inherited and of which he was guardian.

Warmed by the spring sunshine, he sat in the open carriage looking at the new grass, the first leaves on the birch trees, and the first puffs of white cloud floating across the clear blue sky. He wasn't thinking about anything in particular, but gazed around cheerfully and absent-mindedly.

They crossed the ferry where he had talked with Pierre the year before. They went through the muddy village, past threshing floors and green fields of winter rye, downhill where snow still lingered near the bridge, uphill where the clay had been liquefied by rain, past strips of stubble and bushes touched with green here and there, and into a birch forest that lined both sides of the road. In the forest it was almost hot — no wind could be felt. The birches with their sticky green leaves stood motionless, and lilac flowers and the first blades of green grass pushed up through last year's fallen leaves. The dark evergreen of the small fir trees scattered among the birches was an unwelcome reminder of winter. Entering the forest, the horses began to snort and broke into a visible sweat.
Peter, the footman, said something to the coachman; the latter agreed. But apparently the coachman's agreement wasn't enough for Peter, who turned on the box toward his master.
"How pleasant it is, your excellency!" he said with a respectful smile.
"What?"
"It's pleasant, your excellency!"

"What is he talking about?" thought Prince Andrew. "Oh — the spring, I suppose," he thought, glancing around. "Yes, everything is green already. How early! The birches, the cherry trees, and the alders too are coming out. But the oaks show no sign yet. Ah — there's one!"

At the edge of the road stood an oak. Probably ten times the age of the birch trees that formed the forest, it was ten times as thick and twice as tall. It was an enormous tree, its girth twice what a man could embrace, and clearly long ago some of its branches had been broken off and its bark scarred. With its huge, ungainly limbs sprawling asymmetrically, its gnarled hands and fingers, it stood like an aged, stern, scornful giant among the smiling birch trees. Only the dead-looking evergreen firs scattered through the forest and this oak refused to yield to the charm of spring or acknowledge either the sunshine or the season.

"Spring, love, happiness!" this oak seemed to say. "Aren't you tired of that stupid, meaningless, endlessly repeated fraud? Always the same, and always a sham. There is no spring, no sun, no happiness! Look at those stunted dead firs — always the same. And look at me, sticking out my broken and scarred limbs wherever they've grown — from my back, from my sides. As they grew, so I stand — and I don't believe in your hopes and your lies."

As he drove through the forest, Prince Andrew turned several times to look at that oak, as if expecting something from it. Under the oak too there were flowers and grass, but it stood among them scowling, rigid, misshapen, and grim as ever.
"Yes, the oak is right — a thousand times right," thought Prince Andrew. "Let others — the young — fall for that fraud again, but we know life. Our life is finished!"

A whole sequence of new thoughts — hopeless but strangely pleasant in their melancholy — rose in his mind in connection with that tree. During this journey he reconsidered his life, as it were, from scratch, and arrived at his old conclusion — comforting in its hopelessness: that there was nothing for him to begin, that he must simply live out his days, content to do no harm, and not troubling himself or wishing for anything.
